Nifty Options EDA: What Can the Data Answer, and What Is Missing?¶

This notebook explores the local Nifty Options Data in this repository and documents the processing steps, observed statistics, data challenges, and implications for modeling. Its main goal is to assess whether these data can support the project's neural option pricing model and LLM-assisted validation. Historical experiments described in the source document serve only as project background; this analysis does not rerun neural network training or LLM experiments.

The unit of analysis is a record after removing duplicate CSV/TXT representations of the same archived source file. Each row records a price at one time point in a source file. Archive year and month are retained as provenance, rather than assumed to be the actual trading month or expiry month. All raw files are read-only, and this notebook does not upload data.

Reading order¶

  1. Reproduction and file inventory; 2. Excluding duplicate CSV/TXT representations; 3. Explicit parsing of headerless files, 8/9 columns, and different contract symbols;
  2. Full-data quality checks; 5. Actual date coverage and archive months; 6. Prices, quantities, and minute gaps; 7. Modeling limitations and next steps.

To reproduce: run conda activate ./.conda at the repository root, start python -m jupyterlab, open this file, and select the environment's Python kernel. By default, the notebook reads existing results; it runs the analysis script automatically if the summary is missing. After changing the raw data, set REBUILD = True in the next cell to rebuild the inventory and statistics completely.

Equivalent terminal commands (read raw data and write local outputs to data/processed/nifty_eda/ and reports/nifty_eda/):

python scripts/nifty_inventory.py
python scripts/nifty_eda.py
In [1]:

import re

import pandas as pd

# Support starting from either the repository root or notebooks/.

    p for p in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents]
    if (p / 'scripts/nifty_inventory.py').exists()
)
RAW = ROOT / 'Nifty Options Data'
OUT = ROOT / 'reports/nifty_eda'

1. File Inventory: Build an Auditable Manifest First¶

Recursively enumerate CSV/TXT files and record each file's relative path, byte size, SHA256, nonempty row count, field counts per row, symbol formats, and first/last timestamps. This stage examines file contents instead of inferring the schema from the extension. Dates in the first and last rows are preliminary diagnostics; the true minimum and maximum trading dates are computed in the second stage after parsing every row.

Here, canonical_id = archive year / archive month / file stem is only a provenance grouping key, not a verified exchange contract identifier. File counts, row counts, and date counts answer different questions. The total number of records is not the number of independent training examples.

Four observed findings at a glance¶

  • 12,668,930 raw rows belong to file representations verified to be identical, or 41.84% of raw rows on disk.
  • Within the selected data, 2.25% of records have zero quantity, and 19.01% have identical OHLC prices. These measures can overlap and cannot simply be added; they motivate investigation of label quality and trading activity.
  • Only 263,423 rows have a parseable date token in the symbol. For the remaining records, folder names alone cannot reliably establish time to expiry.
  • 2,631,303 rows contain a ninth field. These must be distinguished from the eight-field periods, and the source must still confirm the field's meaning.

Basic quality issues requiring priority review: OHLC inconsistency: 2,952 rows. These records have been flagged and counted but remain in the distribution statistics; they were not automatically deleted or repaired. The counts may overlap and cannot be added to obtain the total number of affected rows.

2. Excluding Duplicate Representations: Do Not Count Both CSV and TXT¶

First compare SHA256 hashes for CSV and TXT files sharing the same archive year-month and file stem. They are treated as duplicate representations of the same source file only when their bytes are identical. Prefer CSV; retain TXT when it is the only format. If contents differ within a group, the script retains the different contents and flags them for review to avoid silently losing data. Identical contents under different provenance keys are not automatically deduplicated across contracts.

This is selection for analysis; no raw files were deleted. Separate checks then examine duplicate rows within source files, candidate contract-time key collisions within each archive, and overlaps across archives at the date, option-type, and strike level. Because most symbols lack a complete expiry date, do not casually deduplicate on date + time + strike + CE/PE: options with different expiries can share those values.

In [3]:
# Reproduce the selection rule using raw-byte hashes and check agreement with the analysis.
recomputed = (
    inventory.assign(_prefer_csv=inventory['suffix'].ne('.csv'))
    .sort_values(['canonical_id', 'sha256', '_prefer_csv', 'relative_path'])
    .drop_duplicates(['canonical_id', 'sha256'], keep='first')
)
assert set(recomputed['relative_path']) == set(selected['relative_path'])
assert int(selected['nonempty_lines'].sum()) == inventory_summary['selected_nonempty_rows']

display(pd.Series(inventory_summary['pair_status_group_counts'], name='Provenance group count').to_frame())
print('Provenance groups requiring manual review:', len(inventory_summary['selection_needs_review_groups']))
print('Identical-byte groups across different provenance keys:', inventory_summary['cross_canonical_identical_hash_groups'])

3. Explicit Schema: No Headers, 8/9 Columns, and Three Symbol Formats¶

The raw files have no headers. Using pd.read_csv(path) directly would treat the first record as column names and lose that row. Specify nine column names for every file, parse the first eight consistently by position, and leave the ninth column missing for eight-column files. The OHLC, quantity, and other meanings below are working interpretations based on field order and contents, not an obtained vendor data dictionary.

Position Working column name Interpretation and treatment
1 symbol Preserve the raw string, then parse CE/PE and strike
2 date Raw date, explicitly parsed as YYYY/MM/DD
3 time Raw time, explicitly parsed as HH:MM; timezone requires vendor confirmation
4–7 open, high, low, close Price fields with an OHLC structure; these are not bid/ask and cannot be used to construct a midpoint
8 volume A quantity field provisionally called trading volume; its units and whether it counts lots remain unconfirmed
9 extra_field_9 A numeric field added for some periods; its meaning is unconfirmed and it is not automatically treated as open interest

Key reading options: header=None prevents losing the first row; names=... aligns files with 8/9 columns; dtype='string' initially preserves raw text; errors='coerce', combined with explicit failure counts, makes conversion failures visible as quality issues instead of implicit format changes.

Do not apply dropna() indiscriminately across all columns: the missing ninth column reflects a file-format change rather than random omissions under one schema. Doing so would systematically remove eight-field periods and change the sample's mix of years and market conditions. NSE's official end-of-day field documentation distinguishes traded quantity/contract counts from open interest. It helps explain why field units matter, but it is not the vendor dictionary for these minute files and does not justify naming the ninth field OI.

The nine-field files in this dataset are concentrated in the 2020-09 through 2020-12 archive cohorts, and include trading dates as early as 2020-07-27. The schema-change chart therefore uses archive cohorts. It would be incorrect to state that only trading records from September 2020 onward have a ninth field; different archive cohorts can also include the same trading date with different coverage.

In [4]:
SCHEMA = ['symbol', 'date', 'time', 'open', 'high', 'low', 'close', 'volume', 'extra_field_9']

def read_example(relative_path, nrows=5):
    # Read-only example; scripts/nifty_eda.py performs full-data aggregation file by file.
    df = pd.read_csv(
        RAW / relative_path, header=None, names=SCHEMA,
        dtype='string', index_col=False, nrows=nrows,
    )
    df['timestamp'] = pd.to_datetime(
        df['date'].str.strip() + ' ' + df['time'].str.strip(),
        format='%Y/%m/%d %H:%M', errors='coerce',
    )
    for col in SCHEMA[3:]:
        df[col] = pd.to_numeric(df[col], errors='coerce')
    return df

3.1 Why Symbol Parsing Cannot Simply Remove All Letters¶

The data contain formats such as CE 8700, NIFTY10000PE, and NIFTY25JUN209800CE. The last format includes the date token 25JUN20; joining all digits into a strike would produce an incorrect result. Match the date-token + strike + type format first, then the formats without a date.

A date token is observable only in symbols that contain one. Its presence in some symbols does not establish verified expiry dates for all files. Archive folder months and filenames alone do not establish actual expiry dates either. A contract master or a reliable expiry mapping is still required before modeling.

The NSE circular dated 2019-01-07 announced the introduction of NIFTY index weekly options from 2019-02-11. This establishes the real possibility of different expiry series during the period covered by these data: strike + CE/PE cannot identify a complete contract on its own. The historical circular does not establish the specific expiry date of each local file, and is not used here to infer expiry rules for all years or for the present day.

In [5]:
def parse_symbol_example(symbol):
    symbol = str(symbol).strip().upper()
    patterns = [
        r'NIFTY(?P<date_token>[0-9]{2}[A-Z]{3}[0-9]{2})(?P<strike>[0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]+)?)(?P<option_type>CE|PE)',
        r'NIFTY(?P<strike>[0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]+)?)(?P<option_type>CE|PE)',
        r'(?P<option_type>CE|PE)\s+(?P<strike>[0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]+)?)',
    ]
    for pattern in patterns:
        match = re.fullmatch(pattern, symbol)
        if match:
            values = match.groupdict()
            return {
                'symbol': symbol, 'option_type': values['option_type'],
                'strike': float(values['strike']), 'date_token': values.get('date_token'),
            }
    return {'symbol': symbol, 'option_type': None, 'strike': np.nan, 'date_token': None}

for style in inventory_summary['selected_symbol_style_row_counts']:

    source = selected.loc[match].iloc[0]
    example_symbols.append(next(iter(json.loads(source['symbols_json']))))

4. Full-Data Quality Audit: Flag First, Then Decide How to Clean¶

Scan all selected files, compute statistics file by file, and then aggregate them, avoiding the need to concatenate more than 17 million records containing strings in memory at once. Basic counts, quality proportions, and numeric quantiles use all records. Quantiles are calculated from exact value frequencies using NumPy's linear interpolation definition, not approximated by sampling. Only the price/quantity distribution chart uses a globally uniform priority sample (100,000 rows, random seed 20261012); the other six figures use full-data summaries. This stage does not automatically delete all anomalies or replace missing values with zero.

Main checks and their meaning:

  • Parsing completeness: failed timestamp parsing, missing numeric values, and unrecognized symbols; interpret these separately from a column that was absent in the original schema.
  • Price consistency: any negative price, a nonpositive close, high < low, or open/close outside [low, high]; flag violations as data issues.
  • Quantity consistency: negative values require review. Zero quantity may represent no trade, a stale price, or a vendor-filled record; zero alone does not justify deletion.
  • Duplicates and ordering: exact duplicates, duplicate timestamp keys, and backward time steps within files; candidate-key collisions within an archive and coarse overlaps across archives are audited separately.
  • Time completeness: gaps between adjacent timestamps within the same source file and date. Gaps are not equivalent to missing trades, and do not establish that the exchange omitted data.

Quality metrics can overlap: one row may trigger multiple rules, so anomaly counts across columns cannot simply be added to obtain the total number of anomalous rows. The absent ninth field in eight-column files is structural missingness and must not all be interpreted as random missingness.

4.1 Investigating Anomalies: Locate the Source Cohort, Then Check the Raw Record¶

An overall proportion can hide the concentration of an issue in a particular data package. The next cell aggregates the existing file-level quality table by archive cohort and shows two denominators: the cohort's share of all zero-quantity records, and zero quantity as a share of that cohort's records. This helps distinguish a broadly observed market pattern from one unusually prominent source cohort, although concentration alone cannot establish the cause.

In [7]:
file_quality = pd.read_csv(ROOT / 'data/processed/nifty_eda/file_quality.csv')
zero_by_cohort = file_quality.groupby('archive_cohort')[['rows', 'zero_volume']].sum()
zero_by_cohort['share_of_all_zero_volume_pct'] = 100 * zero_by_cohort['zero_volume'] / q['zero_volume']
zero_by_cohort['within_cohort_zero_volume_pct'] = 100 * zero_by_cohort['zero_volume'] / zero_by_cohort['rows']
display(zero_by_cohort.nlargest(8, 'zero_volume'))
march_2018 = zero_by_cohort.loc['2018-03']
display(Markdown(
    f"Of all **{q['zero_volume']:,}** zero-quantity records, **{int(march_2018['zero_volume']):,}** come from the 2018-03 archive, "
    f"representing **{march_2018['share_of_all_zero_volume_pct']:.2f}%** of all zero-quantity records. "
    f"That archive contains **{int(march_2018['rows']):,}** rows, with a within-cohort zero-quantity share of "
    f"**{march_2018['within_cohort_zero_volume_pct']:.2f}%**. "
    "Prioritize investigation of bar construction and filling in this source cohort; the finding does not directly imply generally low liquidity throughout the full period."
))

# Locate the raw file from saved quality examples, then read back this line without modifying it.
from itertools import islice

quality_examples = pd.read_csv(ROOT / 'data/processed/nifty_eda/quality_examples.csv', dtype=str)

    quality_examples['issue'].eq('ohlc_inconsistent')
    & quality_examples['symbol'].eq('CE 8700')
    & quality_examples['date'].eq('2017/03/28')
    & quality_examples['time'].eq('16:01')
].iloc[0]
source_line = int(example['source_row'])
with (RAW / example['relative_path']).open(encoding='utf-8') as stream:
    raw_example_line = next(islice(stream, source_line - 1, source_line)).strip()
print('Source:', example['relative_path'], '| Raw line number:', source_line)
print('Raw content:', raw_example_line)
display(example[['symbol', 'date', 'time', 'open', 'high', 'low', 'close', 'volume']].to_frame('Raw value'))

))

This record has O=H=L=414.90, but C=405.80 is below low; quantity is 0 and the time is 16:01. It triggers three checks simultaneously: OHLC inconsistency, zero quantity, and a timestamp outside the reference window. This illustrates why anomaly counts cannot simply be added. Under the working schema, interpreting these four columns as OHLC for the same bar yields an inconsistency. However, the meaning of time, quantity, and price may also depend on vendor conventions for settlement/closing records, so the original data dictionary must be checked. No speculative price repair was made; the original row remains available for review.

4.2 Weekend Records: Investigate Dates Instead of Automatically Deleting by Weekday¶

weekend_observation is a calendar flag, not an error label. First show the weekend dates with actual records, their row counts, and source-file counts, then check historical special trading days and vendor timestamp conventions. Special sessions cannot be excluded indiscriminately using an ordinary weekday rule.

  • 2020-02-01: NSE/FAOP/43291, dated 2020-01-22 explicitly schedules futures and options trading from 09:15–15:30 on the Saturday budget day. Records for this date therefore cannot be deleted solely because it was a weekend.
  • 2020-11-14: Section "1.6 Futures and Options Segment" of the NSE 2020–21 Annual Report records a special Muhurat trading session on this date, demonstrating that ordinary intraday reference windows must also allow for special arrangements.
  • 2019-10-27: A broker-hosted PDF mirror of NSE/FAOP/42404 specifies futures and options Muhurat trading from 18:15–19:15. The original NSE-domain URL could not be read during this analysis, so this source is explicitly identified as a third-party mirror of the original circular, not evidence retrieved directly from the NSE domain.

These official materials establish trading arrangements for particular dates. They do not validate every local price record, its timezone, or its time label, and do not establish that data coverage on those dates is complete.

5. Date Coverage: Distinguish Archive Month, Trading Month, and Contract Identity¶

A monthly package may contain trading records from preceding months. A missing monthly package therefore does not mean that the entire trading month's data are absent; conversely, finding some records for a trading date does not establish complete coverage of that date.

coverage_by_archive.csv compares source months with actual minimum/maximum dates. daily_activity.csv and monthly_activity.csv aggregate using the actual trading dates in the records. Different contracts observed on the same day are highly related. More rows may reflect more strikes, more source files, or denser observations, rather than more independent market states.

This analysis does not automatically treat every weekday as an expected trading day. Until a historical trading calendar is incorporated, weekends, holidays, special sessions, and genuine data gaps must be distinguished.

5.1 Candidate Contract-Key Collisions Are Not Duplicates That Can Be Automatically Deleted¶

Within-archive check: within each archive month, identify records sharing timestamp + CE/PE + strike, and count the affected rows and conflicting values. This finds suspicious overlaps within an archive. It does not perform full timestamp-key deduplication across all archives.

Cross-archive preliminary check: determine whether actual date + CE/PE + strike appears in multiple archive months. The granularity is a day, not a complete timestamp. This can indicate potential overlaps or multiple expiry series, but does not directly give a count of duplicate quotes. Without complete contract identity, equal or different prices are not treated as proof of the same or different contracts.

6. Prices, Quantity, Call/Put, and Minute Coverage Density¶

Price distributions, strike distributions, and CE/PE sample counts can help identify skew and differences in coverage. However, an overall mean price that mixes different years, strikes, expiry structures, and liquidity levels cannot simply be interpreted as the same product becoming more expensive. The ratio of Call to Put records is not a conclusion about bullish or bearish market sentiment either.

Similarly, strike alone cannot determine ATM/ITM/OTM: the underlying price at the same timestamp (or a clearly defined forward price) is required. Without bid/ask, the actual quoted spread or midpoint cannot be calculated either; high-low must not be treated as the bid-ask spread.

6.1 Definitions of Minute Gaps and Coverage Density¶

One-minute data do not mean that every contract has a complete minute grid on every trading day. The analysis calculates gaps between consecutive records within the same file and the same day, so that overnight intervals are not incorrectly reported as missing minutes. The reference window for coverage density is 09:15–15:29, containing 375 minute positions. The denominator consists of dates on which the file has any observation, and the numerator is the number of distinct minutes actually observed within the reference window on that date; dates with no observations at all are excluded from this denominator. This is a diagnostic window, not a verified historical exchange trading schedule. Records outside the window or on weekends require special trading arrangements or vendor documentation before they can be classified. Coverage density is not equivalent to trading volume or the vendor's missing-data rate.

When zero-quantity rows or long gaps are observed, retain their flags first. Do not forward-fill unconditionally: this would manufacture observed prices and could misrepresent a period without trades as actual trading. When comparing different years, also account for changes in record coverage and the schema change caused by the addition of the ninth field.

8. Difficulties Encountered and How They Were Handled¶

Difficulty Consequences if ignored Treatment in this analysis Evidence still needed
The same data are available in both CSV and TXT Double counting and copied samples across training/test sets Compare SHA256 within each source group and select unique content group by group Any future CSV/TXT pairs with different content must be reviewed
No headers and either 8 or 9 columns Loss of the first record, misaligned columns, or treating missing values as zero Specify nine columns explicitly and distinguish structural missingness in the ninth column The vendor's original schema, especially the meaning of the ninth column
Three symbol formats Date digits mistaken for strike and incorrect Call/Put classification Parse each format with regular expressions, prioritizing the date token Complete expiry dates, contract codes, and units
Archive months differ from trading months Incorrect assessment of time coverage and leakage from folder-based splits Use actual row-level timestamps and retain source months separately The mapping between original archives and contracts
Discontinuous minute records and potentially zero quantity Stale prices or filled rows treated as independent, valid labels Measure gaps, coverage density, the zero-quantity proportion, and the proportion with unchanged prices Whether the data represent trade bars, quote bars, or vendor-filled records
No spot, bid/ask, or complete expiry provided Reliable moneyness, DTE, and midpoint cannot be constructed State the field gaps explicitly without fabricating inputs or labels Synchronized underlying prices, a contract master table, interest rates/dividends, etc.
Original files total approximately 1.73 GB Loading everything into a string DataFrame at once requires much more memory than the file size Process files individually, cache results, and have the notebook read summaries by default For larger datasets, consider incremental writes to partitioned Parquet

Some of these issues have been resolved through engineering measures, such as duplicate representations and inconsistent column counts. Others reflect information missing from the data themselves, such as complete expiry dates and synchronized underlying prices. A more complex model cannot automatically turn the latter into real data.

9. Implications for the Project and the Order of Next Steps¶

What can already be done¶

  • Study the quality, trading-time coverage, quantity/price distributions, and anomaly patterns of the actual files; retain reproducible audit evidence for subsequent data adapters.
  • Once the data semantics are clear, try simple time-series baselines using only information available at the time; metrics must distinguish the overall sample from low-liquidity/high-volatility subsets.
  • Have a subsequent LLM select existing, verifiable subsets of historical records as candidates for stress testing; this analysis performed EDA only and did not run an LLM evaluation or establish its effectiveness.

Recommended order for continuing¶

  1. Verify the data dictionary: OHLC/quantity units, timezone, the ninth column, and bar construction, especially the meaning of zero-quantity rows.
  2. Complete contract identity and underlying prices: actual expiry dates, call/put, strike, and synchronized underlying prices; add historical interest rates and dividend/forward information as needed.
  3. Define the label: if the data are trade OHLC, a trade price at a clearly specified time can be studied; quote approximation requires bid/ask, and close cannot simply be renamed midpoint.
  4. Define cleaning rules and retain an audit trail: record every exclusion reason, retention rates by year, and distributions before and after cleaning; do not automatically fill all gaps in time.
  5. Split by actual time: first fix consecutive date intervals for training, validation, and final testing, keeping all contracts from the same day in the same partition. Feature windows or label windows that span days require separation intervals to prevent the use of future information.
  6. Complete simple baselines before introducing an LLM: the independent test set must not be used for model selection or LLM feedback. IV inferred from the same target price cannot be treated as an unconditionally available input.

Through 2018 / 2019 / 2020 can serve as a candidate design for year-based splits, but this EDA has already examined all years, so those years can no longer be described as a previously unseen final sample. In addition, schema, coverage, and market conditions may differ across years, so each partition should be audited separately after splitting. A strict evaluation of a method developed through repeated tuning requires a separate data period that has not been used for exploration.

Relationship to the project background: the historical Black–Scholes synthetic labels are theoretical reference values generated under assumptions; the local market records are a different object of study. These statistics do not establish that market prices should equal Black–Scholes values, nor do they verify that any pricing network or LLM has outperformed a baseline.

10. Outputs and Reproducibility Boundaries¶

  • scripts/nifty_inventory.py: read-only file auditing and CSV/TXT selection.
  • scripts/nifty_eda.py: full-data quality checks, time coverage, and distribution summaries, processed file by file.
  • data/processed/nifty_eda/file_inventory.csv: local file-level inventory, including provenance and hashes.
  • reports/nifty_eda/inventory_summary.json: summary of file selection and the schema audit.
  • reports/nifty_eda/summary.json: full-data EDA summary; consult the actual script and this file for detailed definitions.
  • reports/nifty_eda/tables/: statistical tables that can be checked; figures/: saved figures.
  • This notebook: explains the analysis steps, key statistics, difficulties, and modeling boundaries; it can be rerun.

Reading cached results by default does not detect whether the original files have changed. After adding, replacing, or renaming original files, set REBUILD = True; rerunning only the notebook's display cells does not replace rescanning the data. All conclusions about duplicates, missingness, anomalies, and similar issues are subject to the statistical definitions and scope described above.
